Oct 1, 2014 9:25:32 GMT -5 waxy said:
.
I remember reading on the UK forum about a huge plant of S. flava being found in a very secluded wetland area surrounded by woods on a central parcel of a large farm in the English countryside.....

Now here in the states all bets are off. I've seen a local yokel post that he has planted non-native sarracenia and hybrids in the new Jersey Pine Barrens "just to piss-off the conservationists and biologists". And I have an entomologist friend who says he has seen "tall pitcher plants" down there. I'm trying to get him to show me where.

....but who knows what is in the mud on visitor's boots now, as they travel from site to site.....


Waxy, the point you raise about material on footwear (and by extension, clothing) is utterly valid. Conceivably seed trapped in the upturned cuff of a pair of trousers or a shirt could be unintentionally delivered to the wild from a greenhouse. Again, here in NZ, we have some significant instances where invasive organisms have made ingress into new habitats via boots and waders. In the case of waders many lakes previous free from particular exotic water weeds, particularly Elodea and water net, Hydrodictyon reticulatum, have become choked and the invasion of the diatom, Didymosphenia geminata, remains an enormous threat to our flowing water courses. All users of the water bodies, notably fishers, are officially urged to meticulously clean waders following immersion in one before entering another.

As for that guy introducing plants to the Pine Barrens? What a fool. As you say, it'd be great to find out where and whip them out of there. On that, are there efforts to keep the Pine Barrens as "pure" as possible over all or are they in fact full of a wide range of introduced plants? I know little about them other than Chrissy and Paulie Walnuts chasing a Russian through the snow....

And, that is a really interesting story on the English S. flava.

posts.body_html:
Earl The New Jersey Pinelands National Reserve contains approximately 1,100,000 acres (4,500 km2) of land, and occupies 22% of New Jersey's land area, including territory of much of seven counties. This is just the reserve, the whole ecological zone (including surrounding towns and developed and undeveloped land) is very roughly 5000 square miles, 125 miles N/S by 40 miles E/W, about half the state. The maximum elevation is about 100 feet above sea level. A large part of the pinelands is protected by state and federal legislation. The New Jersey Pinelands Commission is an organization that oversees the management of the outer, Protection Area of the pinelands, and the inner, Preservation Area. map 1 and map 2


This is a huge piece of real estate and it would be impossible to find a few scattered plants unless you had some idea where to look. That was the gist of the individual's taunt. You can never find them on your own. Even with modern technology today, there is a very real danger, that an unfamiliar individual could walk in (or be dropped off, a la Sopranos) and never be seen again. This, a half hour away from the most densely populated region in the country. It is believed even the pre-Columbian natives rarely ventured in. Too dangerous and too unproductive to be worth the risk.
 N.PineBarrens-aerial-NJ Forest Service  and  google images - pine barrens


That is one reason I want my friend to show me where he stumbled on the “huntsman’s horns” (as he called them) while doing an insect study. The various NJ State conservation and preservation groups would remove them. We do have a state invasive species taskforce and in the preservation area non-native plants are prohibited even for landscaping. They’re very serious about it. It is protected at both the federal and state levels. But you can’t be everywhere to police it and anti-social, anti-government miscreants know that.

As for the English flava item, I'm trying to see if I can find it again. I will post a link if I do.


I don't think seed from a greenhouse is as much a concern as visiting three or four widely separated populations a day and distributing seed bank samples among them. If the cloven hooves of deer or cattle can distribute seed, much more so the treaded soles of boots.
